"The lighthouse keeper climbed the spiral stairs each evening, his boots ringing against salt-worn stone. At the top, he polished the great lens until it caught the dying sun and threw a golden fan across the sea. Below, the waves hammered the rocks, and gulls screamed like children lost in the fog.

His name was Elias, and he had kept the light for thirty-one years. The mainland had promised automation, but the island council delayed the order, and Elias delayed his own departure. He told himself he was waiting for the new keeper, though no one had come.

One storm, a boat appeared off the shoals, its mast broken, its crew waving a red lantern. Elias lit the emergency flare and shouted into the wind. The beam swept over the water, and the boat turned, limping toward the harbor mouth. When dawn came, the sailors stood on the deck, soaked and silent, and one of them pressed a coin into Elias's palm.

He kept the coin in a tin with his wife's wedding ring. She had died in the winter he first took the post, and the lighthouse had become both his duty and his grief.

Years later, when the machine finally arrived, Elias climbed the stairs one last time. He turned off the old lamp, watched the new light blink to life, and descended into the quiet. The sea still roared, but the tower no longer needed his hands
